one_liner: Kokkos linear BVH for batched kNN/radius search on CPUs and GPUs; single-threaded kNN beats Boost R-tree at 10^7 points.
what_it_does: ArborX builds a binary bounding volume hierarchy over user values held in Kokkos::Views (points, boxes, triangles, segments, spheres and other geometries in any dimension, reached through an IndexableGetter) and answers a whole batch of spatial (intersects) or k-nearest queries in one call. Results come back either as CRS-style values/offsets views or through a user callback per match, and a PerThread overload lets your own Kokkos kernel query the tree. The same headers carry a BruteForce index, an MPI DistributedTree, DBSCAN/DBSCAN* clustering, an experimental minimum spanning tree and moving-least-squares interpolation. It is not a drop-in for boost::geometry::index::rtree or nanoflann: everything is Kokkos Views and execution spaces, queries are batched, and the tree is immutable (you rebuild it to update).
how_it_is_fast: Construction is a linear BVH: object boxes are reduced to a scene box, centroids are mapped to 64-bit Morton codes (the curve is pluggable), sorted, and the hierarchy plus internal boxes are built in one parallel bottom-up pass using Apetrei's agglomerative variant of Karras's 2012 LBVH (one atomic compare-exchange per internal node). The 2020 paper used plain Karras; the current source uses Apetrei. Spatial queries walk the tree stacklessly through 'ropes' (skip links stored at build time), and nearest queries use a short stack that visits the closer child first (after Patwary et al.) and a k-sized max-heap in a preallocated per-query buffer that shrinks the search radius once k hits are found. Queries are pre-sorted by Morton code so neighbouring threads traverse similar nodes, and spatial results use a count-then-fill two-pass scheme or a one-pass scheme when the caller supplies a per-query buffer size.
when_to_use: Batched neighbour search over 10^6-10^7+ points where all queries are known up front (particle neighbour lists, contact detection, mesh-to-mesh data transfer). In the paper's single-thread runs, kNN (k=10) at 10^7 points was about 1.6x (filled) and 2.1x (hollow) faster than Boost's packed R-tree (bars read by the verifier, derived from page data)

Codes already on Kokkos (Trilinos, exascale applications) that need one search code path for OpenMP, CUDA, HIP and SYCL. The paper found one V100 beat a full two-socket POWER9 node except on small problems
Multicore CPU batches: OpenMP strong scaling at n=10^7 (filled case, Table 1) reached 10.5x for construction, 12.2x for spatial search and 12.1x for nearest search on 16 threads
Search over non-point primitives (boxes, triangles, segments, spheres, tetrahedra, rays) in arbitrary dimension, or distributed-memory search through DistributedTree with MPI
when_not_to_use: Small or medium single-threaded problems: in the filled case the paper shows ArborX slower than nanoflann for nearest search from 10^4 to 10^6 points (about 0.58-0.78x of nanoflann). Thread scaling is also poor below roughly 1000 objects per thread, because the Morton sort is the bottleneck (paper section 3.3)
Data that changes by a few inserts or deletes at a time: there is no incremental update API, so every change means rebuilding the tree
Projects that cannot take on Kokkos 4.5+, C++20 and CMake 3.22. ArborX is header-only, but Kokkos must be built and configured for your backend
Construction-dominated workloads on surface-like (hollow) data: Boost's packed R-tree built faster in the paper's hollow case (about 1.02-1.40x of nanoflann vs 0.87-1.12x for ArborX)

One-off queries from host code in a hot loop: each batched query() call sorts the predicates and launches Kokkos kernels, so the fixed cost per call is high. The PerThread overload helps only inside your own kernel

integration.form: header-only (CMake INTERFACE target; configuring generates ArborX_Config.hpp and a version header, so install through CMake rather than copying src/)
integration.dependencies: Kokkos 4.5+ (required). Optional: MPI (DistributedTree), rocThrust (HIP, on by default), oneDPL (SYCL), Trilinos 16+. Tests and benchmarks only: Boost 1.67+ and Google Benchmark 1.5.4+ (auto-fetched)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, CMake 3.22, Kokkos 4.5.00; compiler minimums follow Kokkos, and NVCC must be 11.5+
integration.platforms: any Kokkos backend: Serial, OpenMP, Threads, CUDA, HIP, SYCL. Test failures were reported on aarch64/ppc64le (issue #1196 hang, closed; issue #1241, stack smashing and wrong neighbour lists in v2.0 tests on aarch64)
integration.thread_safety: query() is const and parallelizes the batch itself over the given execution space. A PerThread overload is callable from inside user kernels. Concurrent query() calls from several host threads are not documented

gotchas: Spatial queries default to two traversals (count, then fill). TraversalPolicy::setBufferSize(n) enables one pass: a positive n falls back to two passes when exceeded, a negative n throws. An oversized estimate costs memory; the paper could not run the one-pass variant above 10^6 points in the hollow case
Predicates are Morton-sorted before traversal by default. The paper found this hurt serial hollow-case spatial search at 10^7 points; turn it off with TraversalPolicy::setPredicateSorting(false)

Nearest traversal keeps a fixed 64-entry stack with no bounds check (ArborX_TreeTraversal.hpp). Trees deeper than that, possible in principle with extreme clustering or duplicate Morton codes, are not guarded. This comes from reading the source; I found no issue reporting it

API churn: v2.0 (2025-04-16) removed the APIv1 index interfaces and moved to C++20 and Kokkos 4.5. Several geometries and helpers (Segment, Ellipsoid, MST, attach_indices, DefaultIndexableGetter) still sit in the Experimental namespace. Within one query, the order of spatial results is unspecified
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ArborX over nanoflann or the single-threaded tree siblings (THST, PH-tree, tidwall rtree.c) when you need GPU or multithreaded batched queries, non-point geometry, or kNN at 10^7 scale. nanoflann is lighter (header-only, no Kokkos) and faster single-threaded up to about 10^6 points. Pick Pkd-tree instead when the point set changes through large parallel batch inserts and deletes on a CPU.
verified_claims_summary: The ACM TOMS 2020 paper ran single-threaded Google Benchmark medians on one core of an Intel Xeon E5-2695 v4 (2.1 GHz, CADES) for m = n from 10^4 to 10^7 points, comparing ArborX against Boost.Geometry.Index 1.67.0 (packed R-tree) and nanoflann 3b2065e. Its bar charts (relative to nanoflann) show similar construction times and k=10 nearest search about 1.6x (filled) and 2.1x (hollow) faster than Boost at 10^7 points, but slower than nanoflann below 10^6 in the filled case (bars read by eye, derived from page data). The paper states no compiler, flags or Kokkos version. The repo's bvh_driver still has a Boost R-tree backend (linear<16>, bulk-loaded) but no nanoflann backend.
status_note: Actively developed by an ORNL-led team (v2.1.0 on 2026-04-28, last commit 2026-09-16, a second TOMS paper for v2.0 in 2025) under BSD-3-Clause; easy to vendor as headers, but practical only if you can adopt Kokkos.
